extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary students, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for creating and evaluating novels, focusing on the relation of subject and form, representation of time and space, handling of material, characterization, and the difference between 'telling' and 'showing'. Written as a critical/theoretical treatise with examples from canonical novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of subject and form
rubrics_metrics.description: “The well-made book is the book in which the subject and the form coincide and are indistinguishable — the book in which the matter is all used up in the form, in which the form expresses all the matter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form must be the exact vehicle for the subject; disagreement between form and subject means material is superfluous or wanting. A successful novel makes form and subject inseparable; when they diverge the book fails to do justice to its idea (example: criticisms of War and Peace's loose form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject must be single and expressible
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel needs “A subject, one and whole and irreducible— a novel cannot begin to take shape till it has this for its support.” and “What was the novelist’s intention, in a phrase? If it cannot be put into a phrase it is no subject for a novel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essential unity of the novel’s subject must be graspable succinctly — size or complexity does not excuse lack of unity. Whether simple anecdote or wide network of relationships, the subject should reveal its unity (the form depends on it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must be determined by subject
rubrics_metrics.description: “The form of the book depends on it, and until it is known there is nothing to be said of the form.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You should decide the novel’s form only after clarifying the subject; the form should arise from and serve the subject rather than be an independent ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of material / avoid wastefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy’s novel is criticised as “wasteful of its subject; that is the whole objection to its loose, unstructural form.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use material only insofar as it furthers the subject/design. Importing irrelevant stories or failing to develop a chosen theme wastes potential and weakens the whole picture (anti-pattern: sprawling subplots that dilute the main theme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of scope and population to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subjects (e.g., the march of life, generational shifts) “require… a big and various population” and room; others may need a limited, self-contained world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the size of cast and setting to what the subject demands: representative/epic subjects need a wide world and many figures; intimate subjects may require a closed horizon (examples: Tolstoy’s large population vs. a novel with a tightly-drawn world).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering a convincing sense of space/horizon
rubrics_metrics.description: The book should create either an open world (“daylight seems to well out of his page… there is no perceptible horizon”) or an intentionally closed horizon (Dostoevsky’s ‘curtain of darkness’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether you show an expansive world or a suffocatingly narrow one, the chosen spatial atmosphere must suit the fable and be consistently maintained; description is not the only means — freedom of character movement and implied continuity can produce space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must possess freedom and reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should “move in an atmosphere that knows no limit” and have “such freedom, such an obvious latitude of movement in the open world.” They should be essentially familiar and intelligible, allowing readers to imagine their lives beyond the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters who feel alive and consistent in ways that let readers project them outside of the narrated scenes. Realism does not mean exhaustive description; it can derive from a normal, everyday gift of experience and consistent treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency/truth of character across contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are praised for being “never less than absolutely true to themselves; wherever we meet them, in peace or war, they are always the people we know.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters behave in ways coherent with their nature throughout varied situations; consistency supports verisimilitude even if the author changes zoom or focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the passage of time as form
rubrics_metrics.description: “The form of time is to be represented, and that is something more than to represent its contents in their order.” The movement of the wheel of time must be made perceptible; merely listing events or saying 'years have fled' is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the structure (lines and masses) of the book so that time’s continuity, accumulation, and sweep are palpable. Time’s effects should be shown through changes in characters, texture of thought, gestures, and the build of the whole book rather than episodic timestamps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent both continuous lapse and cyclical sweep of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Time has a “double effect — its uninterrupted lapse, and the cycle of which the chosen stretch is a segment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show both the quiet, incremental passage of years (internal change) and the larger rise-and-fall arc of generations or cycles that give the story its broader meaning; structure should make the curve apparent even if only a segment is narrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must give reason for telling / convey moral/design
rubrics_metrics.description: “The shape of the story must give the reason for telling it, the purpose of the author in chronicling his facts.” Without design, scattered scenes make no picture; the picture itself is the moral only if it is formed by design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure chapters and episodes cohere to announce a single design or meaning; avoid a sequence of scenes that lacks a unifying organising principle. The reader should be able to perceive why these events were chosen and arranged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain authorial purpose and method throughout
rubrics_metrics.description: An author must not vacillate: Tolstoy’s “vacillation prevents [the facts] from expressing” his original reason; changes in attitude/method can fragment the book’s representative character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on an approach (tone, scope, representative intent) and adhere to it so that the material consistently expresses the intended design. Shifts in viewpoint or method can convert a representative work into a mere group-tale and dilute the original theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid converting representative figures into mere romance-centred characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a character (e.g., Natasha) the heroine of a particular romance can “throw away the value that she had” as a representative spirit of youth; the author must preserve the character’s representative function when intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a character is meant to be emblematic (representative of a social type or age), do not subordinate that role to narrower plot entanglements which change their meaning; balance individual incidents with their representative significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and order of material (no rambling)
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist must avoid material that “has rambled and wandered uncontrolled — or controlled only by… consistency in the treatment of his characters.” Excess or disorganization prevents threads from coalescing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise editorial control: ensure episodes, subplots, and digressions serve the main design; otherwise they weaken and divide the overall effect. The presence of great talent does not excuse chaotic planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed subject and deliberate presentation (Flaubert model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flaubert’s Madame Bovary is given as a model: “the subject stands firm and clear… the story stands obediently before the author, with all its developments and illustrations, the characters defined, the small incidents disposed in order.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject is fixed, the novelist’s task becomes how to present it: order incidents, define characters, and craft manner/phrasing to achieve the desired effect. A firm subject allows precise control of method and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show rather than merely tell — create an image
rubrics_metrics.description: “The art of fiction does not begin until the novelist thinks of his story as a matter to be shown… The book is not a row of facts, it is a single image; the facts have no validity in themselves, they are nothing until they have been used.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating the novel as an information list or historical attestation. Use scenes, detail, and form so the story ‘tells itself’ by presentation; rely on internal convincingness (verisimilitude) rather than external sources of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal verisimilitude over external attestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike narrative forms that appeal to outside authority (e.g., Defoe’s historic truthfulness), a novel must “look true” by its own internal presentation; attestation is irrelevant in a strictly fictional novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build truthfulness through consistent internal detail, character behaviour, and structural choices rather than through claims of historical accuracy or external proof.
